title: The services page a law practice actually needs
metaTitle: Law practice services page, in plain words
excerpt: Each service on a law practice services page needs an outcome, a boundary, and a way to request a consultation. Vague capability grids do not help.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out, a display that lets a passerby read the offer the way a services page should.
caption: Titles facing the street, so a person can choose without opening every book. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a law firm name its services online?
faqs.answer: Use the words a client would use for the job in front of them. A shop lease, a letter from another lawyer, or papers for an owner leaving are clearer than department names. You can keep the internal name in a quieter line for referring lawyers.

faqs.question: What should each service block include?
faqs.answer: Include the outcome the client leaves with, the boundary of who it is for and where it stops, and a request for a consultation. Say what to send with that request. A block that only lists capabilities still forces the client to guess.

faqs.question: How many services should the page feature?
faqs.answer: Feature the services you want to be hired for and can keep accurate. A short index can list the rest. If a service has no one in the firm who would update the description, it should not be written as a full promise.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A law practice services page should list the work in the client's language. Each service needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, and that next step is to request a consultation. A grid of vague capabilities gives a hurried client nothing to match against the letter in their hand.

Google's guidance on title links asks for descriptive, concise titles, and it treats repeated boilerplate as a reason a search result becomes hard to tell apart. The same standard belongs on the page itself. "Services" is a drawer. The client needs the names of the jobs inside it. Google's people-first questions ask whether someone leaves having learned enough to act. On this page, acting means knowing whether their matter is one you take.

## Write the list in the client's words

Clients do not arrive saying they need a practice group. They arrive with a document, a person, and a date.

"Commercial leasing" is how the firm files the work. "Review the lease for your shop before you sign or renew" is how the client looks for it. "Dispute resolution" is a department. "Help when a supplier, a customer, or a co-owner has already involved a lawyer" is a situation. "Corporate" is a category. "The papers a small company needs when an owner joins or leaves" is a job.

Use the client's phrase as the heading. You can keep the firm's phrase in a quieter line if referring lawyers search for it. The heading is what a person under time pressure scans. Nielsen Norman Group found that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they open, so the heading has to carry the sort. A clever internal name that requires the paragraph underneath will be missed.

Read the headings aloud as a list, with no paragraphs. A stranger should be able to point at the one that matches their problem. If they cannot, the list is still written for the firm.

## Outcome, boundary, next step

Treat each service as a small block with three parts. Stop when those three are clear. More adjectives do not make a fourth part.

The outcome is what they leave with. A marked-up lease and a short note of the risks. A response to the letter they received. A set of owner documents ready to sign. Name the object. "Peace of mind" is not an outcome they can hold.

The boundary is who the service is for, and where it stops. Independent shops, not large retail chains. Advice on the letter, not a hearing. Companies with a handful of owners, not a public listing. A boundary lets the wrong client leave quickly, which is a service to them and to you.

The next step is a request for a consultation, with the one or two things you need for that service. For a lease, the draft and the deadline. For a letter from another lawyer, the letter and the other party's name. For an owner change, the current agreements if they have them. The button can share one label across the page. The sentence beside it should change, so the request feels specific to the job.

Put those three parts in the same order every time. A client comparing two services on your site should not have to relearn the layout.

## How many blocks to publish

Publish the services you want to be hired for, written in full. Three to six blocks is a range many practices can keep honest. The test is maintenance. If a service changes and nobody would update the block, it should not be on the page in that detail.

A longer index can sit below, in plain links, for matters you do take and do not need to feature. Each link should still name the job. A rare matter with no owner inside the firm is a promise the page should not make.

Order the blocks by the jobs clients arrive with, not by the age of the department or the seniority of the partner who leads it. The first block will be read most. Give that position to the work you want a hurried client to recognize.

If two services always confuse people, split them. Reviewing a lease and negotiating one are different outcomes and often different fees. Merging them into "leasing support" saves a heading and costs a clear boundary.

## One block, written all the way through

Here is a pattern for a lease review, using a fictional shape any firm can replace with its own.

Heading: Review a shop lease before you sign.

Outcome: You get the draft back with comments, plus a short note of the clauses that change your risk, your rent, or your ability to leave.

Boundary: For independent shops and small hospitality businesses. We read the lease you have been sent. We do not negotiate with the landlord unless you ask for that as a separate step. We do not act outside the jurisdictions listed on the page.

Next step: Request a consultation. Send the draft and the date you have been asked to sign.

That block is enough for a client to decide whether to write to you tonight. It does not require a stock photograph of a handshake, and it does not require a Latin heading. The firm's real fee shape can sit in one line under the outcome, or on the pricing page, as long as the two pages do not contradict each other.

Do not invent a client sentence to decorate the block. If you have permission and a real result you are allowed to publish, link it from the proof page. A services block can stand on the outcome and the boundary alone.

Write the next block the same way for a different job. Employment advice on a termination letter. A founder agreement before anyone wires money. An estate plan for a family business. The repetition of the structure is a kindness. The content of each block has to stay specific, or the structure becomes a template the client can see through.

## What a capability grid fails to do

A grid of icons and abstract nouns looks like a full site. Strategic counsel. Tailored solutions. End-to-end support. Trusted advisors. Each cell is short, and each cell could belong to any firm in the city.

Under time pressure, the client is trying to match a fact they hold to a fact you publish. The letter is about a personal guarantee in a lease. The grid says "property." The match fails, and they leave to a firm that used the words personal guarantee.

Icons do not repair the noun. If you want a visual, use it beside a heading that already says the job. The heading does the work. The icon is optional.

The same failure shows up in boilerplate titles. Google notes that titling many pages with the same uninformative text makes it impossible to tell the pages apart, and that vague labels such as "Profile" throw away a chance to say what the page is. Give each service a title element that names the job. "Shop lease reviews" tells a searcher, and a client, what they will get. "Services | The Firm" tells them they have more clicking to do.

## Keep the people nearby, and the costume out

A services page can name the lawyer who usually does that work, with a role and a link. One line is enough. The about page is where the fuller reason to trust that person belongs. Do not turn every service block into a biography, or the outcome gets pushed down.

Leave marble, scales, and Latin off this page. They do not clarify a boundary. A short sentence in plain English will.

Mention related work only when it prevents a wrong hire. If a lease review often reveals an employment clause for the client's staff, you can say so in one line and link that service. A block that tries to upsell every other service becomes the vague grid again, just in paragraphs.

Jurisdiction is part of the boundary, and it belongs in the block when it changes who you can help. A client with a deadline in another state should not discover the limit after they have attached the lease. If you work with a local agent or a barrister for hearings, say that in the boundary too, so the outcome they picture matches the outcome you deliver.

Read the page on a phone. Each block should be understandable without a desktop sidebar. The consultation control should appear in the first screen of the page and again after the block the client actually needs. Repeating the same control is fine. Repeating the same adjective is not.

## Hand the client to a person

A services page proves the work. It does not, by itself, prove that a specific person will stand behind it. After the blocks are clear, the client who is still deciding will look for a name.

Read [how to write the about page](/blog/how-a-law-practice-should-write-an-about-page) next. That page should say who does the work and why this client should care, and it should skip the origin story unless the story changes the decision to request time.

When you want the same standard applied to your own offers, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Each offer should be something a stranger can repeat after one reading.
